extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists and creative writers (particularly those working on novel openings)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating effective first lines for novels: what openings should do, techniques to use (in media res, moral dilemma, short lines, oddball world-building), and anti-patterns to avoid. Includes examples from famous novels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t put too much pressure on your first line
rubrics_metrics.description: Although your opening sentence is really important, putting lots of pressure on your first line is generally counterproductive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can revisit your opening many times as you get to know your plot, setting, and characters. If this is your first draft, take your time — you’ll build up the main character later. ‘Indulge yourself’ at early stages; the perfect first line often emerges after multiple drafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: The first line only needs to start your story
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes, the only thing the first line of a novel really needs to do is start your story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't assume the opening has to contain genius or all the stakes; its primary job can simply be to get the reader into the story. Use it to begin movement into scene, character, or problem rather than to show off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openings should be assured, calm, and steady; resist showing off
rubrics_metrics.description: Openings don’t need to be genius; they need to be assured, calm, and steady. You want to put your reader at ease and into safe hands, and the best way to do that is resist showing off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simply tell us where we are and who is there, and move gently onto what’s at stake. Avoid flashy or self-conscious phrasing that distracts from grounding the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell us what your main character wants and what stops them
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell us what your main character wants. Then, tell us more about the problem—what stops them from getting it? What’s the source of their frustration?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the opening (or the opening scene) to introduce desire and the obstacle; this sets the reader’s expectation for the central conflict early on. This can be explicit or implied, but the sense of want and blockage should be clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider who is telling the story and the agent of change
rubrics_metrics.description: The sentence you choose to start off your novel will probably be influenced by several factors: main themes, the inciting incident, who is telling that story, and the form you are telling it in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match voice and perspective in the opener to narrator choice and the novel’s perspective (e.g., outside observer vs. first-person narrator). The examples show openings shaped by whether the agent of change is a person and whether the narrator is inside or outside the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: If you have a ‘situation’ and a cast set piece, open with the situation
rubrics_metrics.description: When you have a recognisable situation and a cast of characters (a set piece), an effective first line can announce the situation plainly and place characters within it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples like ‘It was love at first sight.’ and Hemingway’s village house opening demonstrate how a clear situational start situates the reader immediately and introduces the ensemble or context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and allegorical novels often begin in media res
rubrics_metrics.description: You might notice that historical and/or allegorical novels often begin in media res to pique the reader’s interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dropping readers straight into action, an unusual circumstance, or a compelling line of narrative (e.g., a wrong number at midnight; a transformation) can quickly create intrigue appropriate to historical or allegorical tones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the ‘after’ (flashforward) to warn and create curiosity
rubrics_metrics.description: There’s nothing to say you can’t start your story with the ‘after,’ and then take us to the ‘before’ and show us how your characters ended up there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Starting with a future consequence (e.g., ‘Many years later, as he faced the firing squad…’) signals stakes and creates a question the narrative will answer, effectively hooking readers with a promise of cause-and-effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: For fantasy and sci‑fi, use oddball first lines to signal difference
rubrics_metrics.description: If you’re looking to build a brave new world for your readers, let them know just how different it is from the outset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A surprising or strange opening (e.g., clocks striking thirteen) quickly signals world rules or tone. Use distinct sensory or conceptual oddities to orient readers to a non‑ordinary setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut to the moral dilemma early
rubrics_metrics.description: Another powerful way to tackle the first line is to expose the novel’s dilemma right away. You might even imply what readers likely suspect: that this is going to change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Openings that foreground a character’s moral position or an ethical situation invite readers to anticipate consequences and character development (example: openings that reveal a solved or ongoing moral problem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Short first lines can be effective and authoritative
rubrics_metrics.description: With a short first line, the reader enters the world you’ve created without delay. It can also lend a sense of authorial confidence and authority that places the reader in safe hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short lines (‘Call me Ishmael.’) accelerate immersion and can convey voice and confidence. Use brevity when it serves tone, authority, or immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid clichéd or overused opening lines (anti‑pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some first lines are widely regarded as examples of what you shouldn’t do in a novel’s opening (e.g., ‘It was a dark and stormy night’).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer clear of tired, melodramatic, or overly ornamental openings that have become clichés. The page highlights this as an anti-pattern and presents it as a commonly mocked example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polish the first chapter (and hook/synopsis) before perfecting the first line
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s likely that you won’t find the perfect first line for your novel until you’ve worked through the hook (one-line premise) and your synopsis a few times, and got to grips with your theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on developing the hook, synopsis, and first chapter; the ideal first line often emerges through revision. The site recommends working through structural elements and drafts before obsessing over the opening sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples from great openings as inspiration and reassurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Studying celebrated opening lines can provide inspiration and show that effective openings range from simple to complex, from short to elaborate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article provides many exemplars across categories (first‑person narrators, outside observers, historical openings, moral dilemmas, oddball sci‑fi/fantasy lines, short lines) to illustrate different successful techniques; emulate the underlying principle rather than copying phrasing.
